newsitem.title: UK: FirstBus gears up for Europe expansion drive.
newsitem.headline: FirstBus gears up for Europe expansion drive.

text.p: British transport group FirstBus Plc is gearing up for an expansion drive into continental Europe -- a market currently in the throes of liberalisation which first began in Britain 10 years ago.
In an interview with Reuters, Trevor Smallwood, FirstBus chairman, outlined plans to transform his national bus and rail operator into a European contender.
British investors have been nursing a passion for transport stocks over the last year, with demand fuelled by the huge opportunities thrown up by European privatisation and deregulation.

The interest began in earnest with Stagecoach Holdings Plc and has since ignited across the sector, with FirstBus seeing its shares rocket from 152 pence a year ago to 228 pence per share in March 1997.

With Stagecoach already well established with operations on the Continent, attention has turned to players like FirstBus which says it is determined to catch up in the drive for Continental bus and rail deals.
FirstBus has overtaken Stagecoach to become the largest bus operator in Britain, with 20 percent market share. It also has stakes in Britain's passenger rail franchises
But it continues to lag behind internationally and has no overseas operations, an issue Smallwood told Reuters it is addressing.
"A lot of other European countries are where we (Britain) were 10-11 years ago -- operating buses which are highly subsidized."
He said British companies were ideally placed to use their experience to cash in on the spoils. But added that the only possible dampener on the continent was cultural.
"The real debate is a cultural one -- will other countries be comfortable with a UK firm taking over."
Smallwood sees the Nordic and Benelux countries showing the most potential and is also examining Spain and Portugal.
But he adds there are still opportunities to be exploited at home.

Smallwood rebuts comments from rivals, including Go-Ahead Group Plc, which recently said it believed FirstBus had paid over the odds for some domestic acquisitions, inflating prices of British bus companies.

"There is obviously a price level above which we would not purchase. Each company has its own characteristics but we think in a lot of cases there is value to be had. There is still ample opportunity to grow earnings per share," he said.

Smallwood said the current uncertainty ahead of the British election, due to be held by May 22, may make prices keener. Recently, FirstBus bought London bus firm CentreWest for 54 million pounds ($86.2 million).
"There are still bargains to be had in the short term as people are uncomfortable about the risks of political uncertainty," Smallwood said.
A change of government is likely with the opposition Labour Party riding high in opinion polls and widely tipped to win the election after 18 years in the political wilderness.
Such a move could herald an overhaul of transport regulation. But FirstBus said it had little to fear from Labour.

The current shadow transport team -- led by Andrew Smith and his deputy Glenda Jackson, the actress-turned-politician -- has been welcomed as a pragmatic change from the more interventionist approach of left-winger Clare Short.
One key shift in approach is that Labour is expected to look more favourably on allowing co-ordination between bus companies on routes and time-tabling, where it benefits the passenger.
"We see short term possibilities in a change of view on partnerships." The industry does not expect fares regulation and says there could be dialogue on having a single regulator for buses and rail.
But Smallwood and others agree that one of the biggest changes could come from greater powers being given to local authorities to manage transport needs.
This would include the power to raise funds through tolling -- money which will theoretically be ring-fenced for spending on local transport.
Smallwood also sees consolidation in the local rail market. "Over the next two to three years I see it consolidating down to five or six groups, of which I think we will be one," he said.

FirstBus shares have seen a rapid rise over the last year, as seen above. Since July 1995, the shares have outperformed the FT All Share index by 27 percent and the transport sector by 29 percent, according to Reuters 3000 data.
Its profits are forecast to rise by 130 percent in the year to March 31 1997 to 50.5 million pounds, rising a further 32 percent to 66.8 million the year after. ($ = 0.626 British Pounds)
